title: The turning of the qiblah
hook: during a prayer the direction turns from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:144)

segments.voice: Yesterday, adhan, and Bilal's voice over the rooftops. Your line was bilal calls. Did you stop, even for ten seconds, at a prayer time? Day two hundred sixty-two.

A small mosque on the edge of Medina. A row of men are in the middle of the afternoon prayer, facing north, toward Jerusalem, the way Muslims have prayed for years. Someone comes in at the door. He's just prayed with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and he calls out: the direction has changed. We've been told to face the Ka'ba in Mecca. And the whole row, in the middle of the prayer, without breaking it, turns around. North to south. Their backs are now where their faces were. A mosque in Medina today carries a name that remembers it: the mosque of the two qiblahs. Today: qiblah.
screen: `MID-PRAYER, FACING JERUSALEM.` → `THE DIRECTION HAS CHANGED.` → `THE WHOLE ROW TURNS.`

segments.voice: The qiblah is the direction Muslims face in prayer. For the first years, including about sixteen or seventeen months in Medina, Sahih al-Bukhari says, the Prophet and his companions prayed toward Jerusalem, toward the holy house there. Commentators connect it with the long line of prophets before him, Abraham, Moses, David, Jesus, whom Muslims count as prophets too. But the hadith says he longed to face the Ka'ba, the house the Qur'an says Abraham and Ishmael raised. The Qur'an describes him turning his face to the sky, and then the verse came, in al-Baqarah: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. Some people objected. Why change? And the Qur'an's answer, two verses earlier, in Pickthall's words, is: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West." Muslim teachers draw the lesson plainly: the direction was never where God is. The qiblah is where the community faces, together, so that people in every place line up toward one point. The next verse adds that the change was also a test: would people follow, even when it was hard to understand? Some followed in the middle of a prayer. And a detail worth keeping: the Qur'an itself says elsewhere that goodness isn't just turning your face east or west, but faith and generosity and keeping your word. The direction matters. It was never the whole thing.
screen: `FIRST, TOWARD JERUSALEM.` · `TURN YOUR FACE TO THE SACRED MOSQUE.` · `EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.` · `NOT ONLY WHICH WAY YOU FACE.` · then, large: `TURN YOUR FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face the qiblah once more. If you know the direction of Mecca from where you are, or can find it on your phone, turn and face it now. Sit, or stand. People praying anywhere on earth face this same point, from every side, like the spokes of a wheel. If you don't know the direction, just turn slowly in a full circle, and recall the verse: unto Allah belong the East and the West. Then sit, facing that way. The bell holds the time.
Qiblah, the direction faced in prayer: changed from Jerusalem to the Ka'ba in Mecca, remembered as a row turning mid-prayer.
Your line: turn your face. Today, when you catch yourself facing the wrong way, toward a grudge or a screen or a worry, turn, physically if it helps. Day two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca for each prayer, finding the direction by mosque niches, compasses or phone apps, and the mosque of the two qiblahs in Medina is visited by many pilgrims.

fork.setup: you're in the middle of a prayer, facing Jerusalem. a man at the door calls out that the qiblah has changed to Mecca. what do you do?
options: stop praying and go find out.
fork.reveal: the row turned around without breaking the prayer. the mosque where it's remembered is called the mosque of the two qiblahs.

original.note: Arabic: the direction faced in prayer. from q-b-l, to face, to meet.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims always faced Mecca.
what it means: for years they faced Jerusalem, then the direction turned to the Ka'ba, and some turned mid-prayer.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 40 and 403 give the change and the turning; which mosque it happened in is told differently, Quba at dawn or Banu Salimah's, now Masjid al-Qiblatayn.

sources.quoted: Unto Allah belong the East and the West.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:144 (turning his face to the sky; turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque)
Qur'an 2:177 (goodness is not only turning east or west)
Sahih al-Bukhari 40, 403 (sixteen or seventeen months; people turning in prayer)

notes: Pickthall's 2:142 phrase quoted from memory; please check.

Which mosque turned mid-prayer: Bukhari 40 mentions a mosque whose people were bowing at 'asr; 403 has Quba at fajr; later tradition names Banu Salimah's mosque (Masjid al-Qiblatayn). The hook tells the afternoon version at the two-qiblah mosque; confirm framing.
'Facing north' is a simplification for Medina toward Jerusalem (roughly north); confirm.
Whether the Meccan-period qiblah was Jerusalem throughout is discussed by scholars (some say he faced both by standing south of the Ka'ba). Kept to 'for the first years'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): narrator's theology ('God is in no direction') now framed as Muslim teaching; the test is attributed to 2:143 itself, not to commentators; 'a million people', 'again and again to the sky', 'many did' and 'a few verses earlier' (it is two) fixed; the honoring of earlier prophets attributed to commentators; Kaaba spelled Ka'ba as elsewhere on the path; the two-qiblah mosque is no longer said to be the original building 'still standing'.
